title: Finite fibre-valuation test for domination of curve modifications
statement: Let $K$ be a separably closed field [def-kun-separably-closed, def-weil-field] and $V\subseteq K$ a valuation ring with fraction field $K$, meaning that for every $b\in K^\times$ either $b$ or $b^{-1}$ belongs to $V$. Assume the prime ideals of $V$ form a finite chain. Put $T=\operatorname{Spec}V$ and $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Let $C$ be a normal $T$-curve with smooth generic fibre [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and finitely many irreducible components; normal means every local ring is an integrally closed domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Let $q:W\to C$ be a modification with reduced source [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. There exists a finite set $F$ of centred valuations on components of $C$, all of residual transcendence degree one and with closed centres on $C$, with the following property: if $p:C^{\prime}\to C$ is a modification, $C^{\prime}$ is normal, and the centre of every $\nu\in F$ on $C^{\prime}$ is a generic point of its $T$-fibre, then there is a unique $C$-morphism $h:C^{\prime}\to W$, and $h$ is a modification. For any modification $p:C^{\prime}\to C$ with reduced source, every centred valuation on $C$ lifts uniquely to $C^{\prime}$. If its centre on $C$ is closed, its centre on $C^{\prime}$ is either a generic point of its $T$-fibre or a closed point of $C^{\prime}$. Finally, if $B$ is a normal $T$-curve with smooth generic fibre and $r:B^{\prime}\to B$ is a modification with reduced source, then $r$ is an isomorphism over a neighbourhood of every generic point of every $T$-fibre of $B$; consequently a valuation centred at such a point stays centred at a generic fibre point on $B^{\prime}$. A $T$-curve means a flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] $T$-scheme of pure relative dimension one [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], with no separatedness or properness assumption. A modification is a proper morphism [def-weil-proper-morphism] inducing an isomorphism between schematically dense open subschemes of source and target. Here $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ is schematically dense if $\mathcal O_X\to j_*\mathcal O_U$ is injective. An $\eta$-modification is a modification which is an isomorphism on the entire generic fibre. For an irreducible component $C_i$ [def-weil-irreducible-components] of a reduced $T$-curve $C$, let $L_i$ be its function field, the local ring at its generic point with the reduced induced scheme structure [def-pc-integral-scheme]. A centred valuation on $C_i$ is a valuation subring $O\subseteq L_i$ together with a $T$-morphism $\nu:\operatorname{Spec}O\to C$ inducing that generic-point map. Its centre is the image of the closed point of $\operatorname{Spec}O$. Put $V_O=O\cap K$ and $\kappa(O)=O/\mathfrak m_O$, $\kappa(V_O)=V_O/\mathfrak m_{V_O}$ [def-weil-residue-field]. It has residual transcendence degree one if $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(V_O)}\kappa(O)=1$ [def-kun-transcendence-degree]. The centre on a modification is the centre of the unique lift of this specified morphism.

proof.text: Take the marking empty in [lem-trf-valuation-horizontal-curve-models]. It applies to every reduced modification in the statement, so its source is again a flat finitely presented $T$-curve with one-dimensional fibres, and the generic-fibre map is an isomorphism. For a centred valuation of a component, its fraction-field point therefore lifts to that component of the modification. The proper and separated extension theorem [lemma-nagata-proper-separated-valuation-extension] extends this to a unique map from the whole valuation spectrum. Hence all centres used below are centres of the specified, uniquely lifted morphisms.

source.place: Section 4.2, opening paragraph and valuative interpretation

proof.text: Use the common valuation spaces and sets $\Gamma$ of [lem-trf-modification-fibre-centre-finite], and set $F=\Gamma_0(W)$. That node asserts its finiteness and residual transcendence degree one; closedness of its centres on $C$ is part of the definition of $\Gamma_0$. Thus this is a finite set of the valuations required in the statement, rather than a set of points on two different models.

Suppose that $p:C'\to C$ satisfies the hypothesis. In the common valuation space this is precisely $F\subseteq\Gamma(C')$. Generalization-stability of $\Gamma(C')$ and the formula of [lem-trf-modification-fibre-centre-finite] give $\Gamma(W)=\operatorname{gen}(F)\cup\Gamma(C)\subseteq\Gamma(C')$, since that formula also includes $\Gamma(C)\subseteq\Gamma(C')$. This step uses actual inclusions of centred valuations, not an inclusion between the underlying point sets of $W$ and $C'$.

Let $U$ be the intersection of the isomorphism opens for $p$ and $q$, and take the schematic closure $Z$ of its diagonal copy in $W\times_C C'$. The opens may be taken quasi-compact since the schemes here are quasi-compact quasi-separated. The closure theorem [sk-lem-nagata-sketch-closure] makes $U$ a schematically dense open of $Z$. On affine opens the closure ideal is a kernel into sections on the reduced scheme $U$, so $Z$ is reduced. Each projection $a:Z\to W$, $b:Z\to C'$ is proper: the ambient projection is a proper base change by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-base-change], and a closed subscheme of its source remains proper by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-proper]. Over $U$ both projections are isomorphisms. Thus these are reduced modifications and, by [lem-trf-valuation-horizontal-curve-models], $Z$ is a $T$-curve.

The image of $z$ in $W_s	imes_{\kappa(s)}C'_s$ is closed by [lem-kun-closed-points-of-product]. The natural map $Z_s	o W_s	imes_{\kappa(s)}C'_s$ is a monomorphism, hence injective on points: it factors through the fibre product over $C_s$ and the closed immersion defining $Z$. The inverse image of that closed singleton is therefore $\{z\}$, so $z$ is closed in $Z_s$. But $
u\in\Gamma(Z)$ makes $z$ the generic point of a one-dimensional component, a contradiction. Consequently $\Gamma(Z)\subseteq\Gamma(C')$.

No irreducible component of a $T$-fibre of $Z$ can be contracted by $b$: [lem-trf-modification-fibre-centre-finite] supplies a valuation centred at its generic point, and step 5 makes its image fibre-generic. A fibre of $b_s$ over a closed point is closed in the one-dimensional scheme $Z_s$; if positive-dimensional it contains a whole component, contradicting noncontraction. A fibre over a generic point contains only generic points of $Z_s$: a nongeneric point is closed in $Z_s$, has finite residue field over $\kappa(s)$, and therefore has closed image by [lem-kun-closed-point-field]. There are only finitely many such generic points. Thus all fibres of $b$ are zero-dimensional. Properness gives local finite type, so [lem-trf-locally-quasi-finite-relative-dimension-zero] makes $b$ locally quasi-finite, and [pqf-lem-proper-lqf-finite] makes it finite.

Apply [lem-trf-finite-birational-normal-iso] componentwise to $b:Z\to C'$. A normal scheme with finitely many irreducible components has disjoint open-and-closed components: a point on two components would give two minimal primes in its local domain. On each component $b$ is finite and birational, its source is integral by the reduced schematic-closure construction, and the target is normal by hypothesis. Hence $b$ is an isomorphism. Define $h=a b^{-1}$. It is a modification, since $a$ is proper and an isomorphism on the schematically dense open $U$. Any other $C$-map agrees with $h$ on $p^{-1}(U)$; separatedness of $W\to C$ and the dense-open uniqueness clause of [sk-lem-nagata-sketch-closure] give equality.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 4.2.3, normality and uniqueness

proof.text: Let $c$ be a closed original centre and $y$ its lifted centre on a reduced modification $Y$. Put $s$ for their common image in $T$. If $y$ is nongeneric in the one-dimensional fibre $Y_s$, it is closed in that fibre. By [lem-kun-closed-point-field], $\kappa(y)$ is finite over $\kappa(s)$, and consequently finite over its intermediate subfield $\kappa(c)$. The same lemma applied to the finite-type $\kappa(c)$-scheme $Y_c$ shows that $y$ is closed in $Y_c$. Since $\{c\}$ is closed in $C$, $Y_c$ is a closed subspace of $Y$, so $y$ is closed in $Y$. This proves the dichotomy without assuming that $s$ is closed in $T$.

source.place: Section 4.2 and Proposition 4.3.1 proof, nongeneric-centre alternative

proof.text: Apply the modification-locus assertion of [lem-trf-modification-fibre-centre-finite] with normal base curve $B$ and reduced modification $r:B'\to B$. Its modification locus $L$ is closed and quasi-finite over $T$. It cannot contain a generic point $x$ of a fibre component of $B$: closedness would force all of that one-dimensional component into $L$, whereas a quasi-finite morphism has finite, zero-dimensional fibres. Therefore $x$ belongs to the open $B\setminus L$ over which $r$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse takes $x$ to a fibre-generic point. The unique valuation lift of step 1 must use that point as its centre, which proves persistence.
